books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

stimulus.text: Postcard view of Hull House, Chicago, early 1900s. The red-brick Hull House complex fills a city street corner: a tall main building with gabled roofs and rows of windows, joined to lower wings stretching down the block, with young trees and a lamppost along the sidewalk and the words “THE HULL HOUSE, CHICAGO” printed in red at the upper right.
stimulus.source_note: Vintage V.O. Hammon (Chicago) postcard of Hull House, early 1900s. Image file: Wikimedia Commons, The Hull House, Chicago (front). Public domain.

options.text: helping immigrants adjust to life in America
keeping immigrants in separate ethnic neighborhoods
options.misconception: Turns help adjusting into a plan to keep people apart.
Gives the settlement workers the nativists' goal.

options.text: training immigrants to return to their home countries
options.misconception: Turns classes for life in America into preparation to leave.

rationales.A: English lessons, childcare, and a kindergarten are tools for living in America, not for leaving it. The settlement house goal was to help immigrants adjust to American city life.
rationales.B: The classes pulled immigrants into American life, not walled them off. Separation was the opposite of the settlement goal.
rationales.C: Restriction was the nativists' demand. Settlement workers answered immigration with aid, not with laws to shut people out.
rationales.D: The lessons taught English for life in Chicago. Nothing here prepares anyone to go back across the ocean.
rationales.general:
Judge the goal by what the work actually did.
1. English lessons help a newcomer speak, work, and vote in America.
2. Childcare and a kindergarten help immigrant families live in the city.
3. Background from the books: settlement houses aimed to aid immigrants, especially immigrant women.
4. So the goal was adjustment to American life, not separation, restriction, or return.
Remember: a reform's goal is the change its daily work tries to make.
